subject: city skyline night
title: What If Every City Switched Off Its Lights for One Night?

scenes.text: What if every city went dark for one night? A third of humanity would see something new.
Light pollution covers the sky for over 80 percent of people on Earth, and 99 percent of Americans and Europeans.
One in three people can't see the Milky Way from home. Tonight, it hangs over every city.
Birds notice first. New York's Tribute in Light draws migrating birds to 150 times normal density, from four kilometres away.
Switch the beams off for 20 minutes and the birds scatter within minutes. A dark night lets the migration through.
Lighting ate about 19 percent of the world's electricity in 2006. One dark night, and the stars come back. They never left.

description:
What if every city switched off its lights for one night? A 2016 atlas in Science Advances found light pollution affects the skies of more than 80 percent of the world's population and 99 percent of people in the United States and Europe, and that one third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. Migrating birds would feel it at once: a seven-year study of New York's Tribute in Light found bird densities 60 to 150 times normal within the beams, with effects reaching 4 kilometres, and when the lights were switched off for about 20 minutes the birds dispersed within minutes. In 2006 the International Energy Agency estimated that lighting took about 19 percent of global electricity.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: When the 1994 earthquake blacked out Los Angeles at 4:30 a.m., some residents reported a strange silvery cloud overhead. It was the Milky Way. Have you ever seen it?
